content: The National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) is a system designed to help countries progressively enhance the availability, quality, and utilization of health workforce data. This is achieved through the monitoring of a standardized set of indicators, which support the attainment of Universal Health Coverage (UHC), Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and other health-related objectives. The NHWA aims to standardize and ensure interoperability of health workforce information systems. The NHWA defines standardized indicators to achieve the following goals: Generate reliable information and evidence on human resources for health (HRH). Enable effective planning, implementation, and monitoring of workforce policies to achieve UHC. Improve the comparability of health workforce data at both national and global levels. The NHWA provides a better understanding of health workforce characteristics, including size and distribution. It strengthens HRH information systems to routinely produce high-quality data and evidence, guiding policy decisions tailored to country-specific needs. This involves collaboration among ministries of health, education, and finance, as well as professional associations, training institutions, and academia. The NHWA also informs priority investments needed to strengthen the health workforce and support UHC. Over time, it enhances the comprehensiveness, quality, and comparability of HRH data, fosters cross-country support for data collection, and facilitates the documentation and sharing of experiences and best practices. The NHWA is relevant to national, regional, and global stakeholders. It enables countries to better collect, analyze, and utilize health workforce data to develop evidence-based policies and plans. This supports global monitoring efforts, including those related to SDGs, UHC, and other global commitments. The NHWA also includes specific indicators on health workforce density and distribution, addressing key policy questions such as resource allocation and workforce migration. The NHWA aligns closely with the health labor market framework for UHC, which provides a comprehensive view of health labor market domains, including education, labor market dynamics, financing, governance, policies, and regulation. This framework addresses critical issues such as geographic distribution imbalances, workforce shortages, migration, evolving workforce demographics, and governance challenges. It also informs policies on workforce production, retention, and regulation, ensuring equitable access to safe, effective, and person-centered health services. The NHWA Handbook is structured modularly, aligned with the health labor market framework. It includes 78 health workforce indicators organized into 10 modules covering education, labor force, and population health needs. These modules correspond to major policy areas required to deliver quality health services. The NHWA implementation is a country-led activity, building on existing national systems to progressively improve the collection, analysis, and use of health workforce data. It involves collaboration among multiple stakeholders and is supported by WHO's Implementation Guide, which outlines eight non-sequential steps across three phases: conceptualization, operationalization, and process revision. To facilitate data collection and use, WHO has developed the NHWA Online Data Platform, enabling countries to record, analyze, and visualize health workforce information. Additionally, the NHWA Web Portal displays aggregated, validated data as a global public good, supporting global reporting and dissemination of harmonized health workforce data. The NHWA was developed through a stepwise process involving consultations with experts from both developed and developing countries, including academics, HRH and information systems specialists, policy planners, international organization experts, and health professionals. WHO and its partners have also developed tools and guidance to support NHWA implementation at the country level.
